speaker: karlgrenke
text: Thank you, Mr. Chair. Good afternoon, everyone. For those watching at home, I'll just introduce myself. I'm Carl Granke, the township planner. And I'll be speaking to these applications. So in this case, as Tom had indicated, we have two minor variance applications affecting two properties. However, the planning report and the presentation has been bundled into a single one since ultimately they are entirely dependent on each other. So in this case, this is an exercise. What we're looking at here is essentially the final piece of a long puzzle that involves the correction of some title issues and the adjustment of lot boundaries to properly position existing buildings on their lot. So this is actually a very unusual minor variance in that it's not intended to accommodate development or new development. It's intended to effectively recognize development that's already there. So in this case, the two properties we have on Rito Avenue, 55 Rito Avenue and 68 4th Street, both are developed, one with a semi-detached and one with an existing single house that's been there for probably about 100 years. The semi is much newer. It was recently discovered, unfortunately, that there's a couple of lot line encroachments. So the house is situated on, partly on the adjoining property and the house and the semi-detached is partially within the municipal road allowance. So over the last, after working staff and agents for all of the property owners have met over the last little while and the solution they found was basically a series of consent applications, severance applications where lot lines on all of these properties were adjusted slightly just to make sure that every house was, every building was on its own lot. Everybody had their own appropriate yard requirement. So that was viewed as, and that consent process was necessary for this to happen. Otherwise, we'd still have that situation where there were these encroachments. So the Lanark County Land Division Committee is the approval authority for the severance applications. They approved and they approved the severance applications, but one of the conditions of these severances was that minor variances be obtained to recognize any, minor variances be obtained to recognize any non-compliances in the lot configurations. So all of these properties are zoned general residential special exception two that allow singles and semi-detached with various setback requirements, lot coverage requirements, and so on. This is a very, this is a longstanding developed area. Everything's always a little bit tight to the lot line. And unfortunately, I don't think it's possible to fix these lot lines and create complying situations that are entirely compliant in zoning. So based on the survey that was completed in support of these applications, there were a number of non-compliances in terms of the lot setbacks that had to be corrected. And that includes for 55 Rideau Street, recognize a reduced interior side yard setback, front yard setback, and also for 6 Nate 4th Street, recognize a reduced exterior side yard setback, reduce the minimum front yard setback, rear yard setback, and increase the maximum lot coverage and reduce the minimum lot area. So a lot of relief that's required, but ultimately this is intended to accommodate development that already exists. So the committee is, so this application is being presented to the committee to as essentially the final condition of the severance approval, the committee has to support these or committee has to approve these variances in order for the development or for the severances to be complete. So the applications were circulated to agencies and neighbors as required by the Planning Act. The only feedback we've received was from the Rideau Valley Conservation Authority that has no objection to either of these applications. We haven't heard from any abutting property owners. Ultimately this layout here I understand is a product of that was negotiated and agreed to by both property owners. They're the ones who'd be the most affected by this. So the committee, when they're looking at a minor variance application, there's four tests outlined under the Planning Act that need to be satisfied. Does this proposal meet the general intent of the official plan? Does this proposal meet the general intent of the zoning bylaw? Is this proposal desirable and appropriate? And is this proposal minor? So I would like to reiterate to the committee that these applications facilitate the reorientation of the lot lines affecting the property. So while the committee should not feel obligated to grant zoning relief to fix a building mistake of many years ago, in the opinion of staff, the broader public interest is better served in this instance by recognizing the requested setbacks, which would allow the completion of the consents and allowing each building to be situated on its own lot. So this would allow the greater use and enjoyment of each lot by its occupants without negative impact on abutting properties. So we're not introducing new development. We're not changing the use on any of the subject properties. At the end of the day, if we left things in place as they are right now, we would have a more substantial zoning issues in terms of these encroachments. So broadly speaking, this is a step in the right direction. The official plan doesn't really get into these sorts of prescriptive details about performance standards, but at the end of the day, it wants to see development that makes sense within its neighborhood. And finally, the final test for the committee is this proposal minor. And at this point, in my opinion, it is minor in that it's recognizing the existing condition. So based on a review of our policies and consideration of this neat plan, this unique planning context, in our opinion, these applications do satisfy the four tests of the Planning Act, and we recommend approval with the condition that with the condition established in the committee's decision for both of them, that this application shall be read to accommodate the placement of structures existing at the time of this decision only. So this application can't be read to accommodate future additions, future that would have to be looked at on its own as if that ever happens in the future, and that can come back to this committee. But in our opinion, these applications are a logical final step to effectively correcting an unusual situation here and allowing the completion of the lot line adjustments. So I'll pause there and I'll turn the floor back to the chair.
